# At a Glance

This document reports how I generated base replacement self-repair (RSR)
data with an open-weights language model, starting from the gold train split
of PMB 5.1.0. "Base" means that the repairs carry no editing expression such
as "I mean" or "actually". These will be added by script in a later step.

The training set now holds 3,489 RSR items, about 500 in each of seven
categories, against 9,486 fluent PMB train sentences, a ratio of about
1 : 2.7.^[PMB 5.1.0 has 9,552 train documents. I hold out 66 of them that
look like a repair on the surface but are not one, such as appositions ("I'm from Wellington, the capital of New Zealand"), lists, and contrasts like "not a nurse,
but a doctor". They are kept for a hard-negative test and appear in no
training data.] This experiment shows that, for this project,
generating RSR data with an LLM is a workable method. Six of the seven
categories meet my quality thresholds through generation and automatic
checks alone, and the seventh, edge label, meets them after I selected its
items by hand. I will therefore build the dev and test sets in the same way.
The Switchboard comparison shows that these data should not be treated as
representative of conversational RSR. Their main use is to train and test
the parser for the proposed representation. The next step is to add editing
expressions.

@sec-why explains why I moved from rules to an LLM, and @sec-data shows what
an item looks like. @sec-generation and @sec-qa describe how the items were
generated and how I judged their quality. @sec-results gives the results. The last section covers
limitations and next steps, and closes with one question on which I would
like your advice (@sec-questions).

# Why I do this {#sec-why}

My first data pipeline was entirely rule-based. Each RSR category needed its
own transformation script, so I had five or six scripts to maintain, and
some categories, such as tense, still needed items written by hand. During
my research proposal presentation, Prof Koller suggested that I consider
generating the data with an LLM instead. Given the workload of the rule-based
system and the number of places where it could go wrong, the suggestion made
a lot of sense.

My aim is therefore two-fold, and the second part depends on the first. I
first want to find out how well an LLM, run on the computing resources
available to me, can generate RSR data. Quality has two sides in this task,
naturalness and correctness, and correctness applies to both ends, the
sentence and its SBN. If the quality is good enough, I will then make LLM
generation the main data source of the project.

Two design principles follow from these aims, and they run through the rest
of the document. The first is about generation. I give the model as much
freedom as possible, so that the results measure the model's own ability. It
is constrained only by its input, a PMB sentence with its SBN and the
category to produce, and by a single tool, a WordNet lookup
(@sec-generation). The second is about quality control, which follows the
rule "selection, not correction". An item that fails a check is dropped and
never fixed, so every item in the data is the model's own output, and the
failure rate becomes evidence of how well the model does the task. To judge
how correct and how natural the items are, I combine three kinds of
evidence: automatic structural checks, manual annotation, and a comparison
with repairs in Switchboard.

# What the data look like {#sec-data}

In early versions of my research proposal, I used "replacement" and
"repair" loosely for the phenomenon as a whole. From now on, RSR stands for
replacement self-repair only, and "repair" means only the part of the
utterance that reflects the speaker's final intention. The repair site is
the place in the gold SBN that the repair changes, such as a concept, a name
or the tense of a verb.

Each item is built from one PMB sentence and its gold SBN. The gold sentence
supplies the repair, and the model invents the reparandum in front of it.
Take the gold sentence "Hebrew is my mother tongue", which becomes "Hebrew
was, is my mother tongue". The two SBNs are shown below.

```sbn
% gold: Hebrew is my mother tongue.
hebrew.n.01
be.v.02             Theme -1 Time +1 Co-Theme +3
time.n.08           EQU now
person.n.01         EQU speaker
mother_tongue.n.01  Creator -1

% RSR: Hebrew was, is my mother tongue.
hebrew.n.01
                    CORRECTION <1
be.v.02             Theme -1 Time +1
time.n.08           TPR now
                    CONJUNCTION <2
be.v.02             Theme -3 Time +1 Co-Theme +3
time.n.08           EQU now
person.n.01         EQU speaker
mother_tongue.n.01  Creator -1
```

If the `CORRECTION` box is deleted, what remains is exactly the gold SBN of
"Hebrew is my mother tongue". The notation is designed so that this holds
for every item, once any placeholder concept is merged back. Because every
item starts from a PMB sentence with a gold SBN, a script can test this
property automatically on each item, and most of the checks in @sec-qa rest
on it.

A good item therefore meets three conditions. The sentence and the SBN are
both correct and agree with each other; deleting the withdrawn version gives
back the gold meaning; and the repair sounds natural to a fluent speaker.

## The seven categories

I defined seven RSR categories, derived from my formalism. Each category is
defined by what the repair replaces in the SBN, which is why the names mix
linguistic terms such as tense with SBN terms such as edge label
(@tbl-categories).

| category | what is replaced in the SBN | example | items |
|---|---|---|---:|
| content word | a concept, by another of the same part of speech that is not a synonym | A baby is sleeping in *the basket*, the cradle. | 500 |
| name | the value of a name | Were these pictures taken *in France*, in Germany? | 500 |
| number | a quantity | The bank lent her *300*, 500 dollars. | 500 |
| temporal | a clock time, day, month or year | I was born *in 1971*, in 1972. | 500 |
| tense | the tense of a verb | Hebrew *was*, is my mother tongue. | 500 |
| forwarding | the subject, with the verb said again | *John hates*, I hate spiders. | 500 |
| edge label | the role between two concepts, or a place relation | He jumped *from*, into the train. / Tom was born *near*, in Boston. | 489 |
| **all** | | | **3,489** |

: The seven RSR categories and their size in the training set. Reparanda are shown in italics. {#tbl-categories}

Two categories need a word of explanation. In forwarding, the speaker
restarts the clause with a new subject and says the verb again. In edge
label, the repaired word is a preposition, and in SBN the change falls on
the role that links two concepts, such as `Source` ("from") and
`Destination` ("into").

With the balanced categories, the differences between them in
the parsing experiments cannot come from differences in training data size.

# Data generation setting {#sec-generation}

@fig-pipeline shows the whole process. This section covers generation, and
@sec-qa covers the checks and annotation that follow.

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-pipeline
%%| fig-cap: "From a PMB entry to the training set."
flowchart LR
  P["PMB entry<br/>+ category"] --> L["LLM<br/>(+ WordNet lookup)"]
  L --> C{"automatic<br/>checks"}
  C -- fail --> X["dropped"]
  C -- pass --> A["six categories:<br/>sample annotated"]
  C -- pass --> S["edge label:<br/>every item judged"]
  A --> T["sampling<br/>(about 500 per category)"]
  S --> T
  T --> D["training set"]
```

From the items that pass, I drew a simple random sample of 500 per category
with a fixed seed. Edge label, with fewer items kept, contributes all of its
489. Before sampling, small surface slips such as letter case and quote
marks were fixed.

## Model and data

I used [Muse-Glimmer-30B](https://huggingface.co/meta-models/Muse-Glimmer-30B),
an open-weights model, on PMB 5.1.0 train gold. I chose it for what the task
needs. It can call an external tool over several turns, which the WordNet
lookup requires, and it returns its answer in a fixed structure that holds
the sentence and the SBN together. As a 30B model, it can also run on a single
GPU of the LST cluster, and because the weights are open, every run can be
repeated on university hardware. All runs use the same sampling
settings.^[Reasoning effort high, temperature 1.0, top-p 0.95, top-k 64,
seed 13.] The results in @sec-results show that the model is up to the task.

## Input and prompt

Each request consists of the prompt and one PMB entry, that is, a gold
sentence and its gold SBN, together with the category to produce. The prompt
is shared by all categories and has three parts.

1. An SBN manual, which tells the model how to annotate a sentence in SBN.
   It is a stand-alone document based on Bos' papers ([2021](https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/Variable-free-Discourse-Representation-Structures-*-Bos/6d3b8e54d183a9fdda186f986b319c55c85a6c06),  [2023](https://aclanthology.org/2023.iwcs-1.20/)) and
   the annotation practice in PMB gold.
2. The repair notation, which explains how to annotate an utterance with RSR
   in the `CORRECTION`–`CONJUNCTION` construction. It is derived from my
   [notation document](https://hongxuzhou.github.io/lct_master_project/).
3. The task, which asks the model to read both sides of the PMB entry and
   add an RSR of the given category to both.

Every example in the prompt was checked automatically for well-formed SBN,
and the PMB documents that supply these examples are excluded from the data.

Within the given category, the model decides everything else: where the
repair occurs, which word it uses as the reparandum, and how the sentence
and the SBN are written. If a sentence offers no suitable site, the prompt
allows the model to decline. It has one attempt per item, with no retry and
no self-check, because retrying until an item passes would hide how often
the model fails.

Two categories have less freedom. For some temporal items and for the place
repairs in edge label, the input also names the site to repair, and these
make up more than half of the final items in both categories. Temporal
needed this because only 297 train documents contain a usable time
expression, so many of them had to yield a second item. The reason for
edge label is given in @sec-edge.

## Tool calling

The model's only tool is a WordNet lookup. Concepts in SBN are WordNet 3.0
synsets, so a concept outside WordNet cannot be represented, and the model
needs a way to check what it writes. The lookup lists the senses of a word
with their definitions and confirms whether a concept exists. It shows no
synonyms or hypernyms and offers no list of candidate replacements, so the
model has to come up with the reparandum itself. I kept the tool this narrow
on purpose. A list of candidates would decide in advance which slips are
believable, and that judgement is part of what I want to test.

# Quality assurance setting {#sec-qa}

Each kind of evidence answers a different question.

1. The automatic checks run on every item and ask whether it is well-formed
   and faithful to its gold SBN. An item that fails is dropped.
2. The manual annotation reads a sample of the items that pass and asks what
   the checks cannot see: whether the SBN is correct and whether the
   repair sounds natural.
3. The Switchboard comparison describes how the generated repairs relate
   to repairs in real speech. 

Whether a category can enter the data is decided by four thresholds
(@tbl-thresholds). 


::: {.callout-caution}

The figures come from my experience as an annotator, as I
know of no established standard for data of this kind.

:::

I fixed them before
seeing any results, so that I could not adjust them to fit.

| evidence | measure | threshold |
|---|---|---:|
| automatic checks | answered items that pass every check | ≥ 95% |
| automatic checks | sentences the model declines | ≤ 3% |
| manual annotation | items correct in meaning | ≥ 90% |
| manual annotation | items that sound natural | ≥ 80% |

: Thresholds for admitting a category. {#tbl-thresholds}

## Structural checks

The checks fall into five groups (@tbl-checks).

| check group | an item fails if |
|---|---|
| well-formed graph | the SBN is not well-formed or has a cycle, a pointer lands on no concept, or a concept is not in WordNet |
| graph returns to gold | deleting the withdrawn version, and merging back any placeholder concept, does not give back exactly the gold SBN, or something away from the repair site has changed |
| sentence and graph agree | the sentence does not match the SBN, for example because the words out of the RSR span are also changed by the model, or the model chooses a reparandum that is identical to the repair (i.e., resulting in a repetition). |
| site within the category | the repair site is not one the category allows, such as one place inside the other ("Osaka, Japan") |
| a repair, not a synonym | the reparandum and the repair belong to the same WordNet synset, as "sofa" and "couch" do; however, a more general or a more specific word is allowed |

: The five groups of automatic checks. {#tbl-checks}

## Manual annotation

From the items that pass every check, I draw 15 per category at random and
read them one at a time, without seeing the category or any check result.
For each item I answer two questions: does the repaired SBN mean what the
repaired sentence says, and is the repair natural? By natural I mean
acceptable to a fluent speaker, that is, grammatical, recognisable as a
repair, and with both versions recoverable. This is different from typical
of speech, which is a question for the Switchboard comparison. Either answer
may be "unsure", and I compute the rates over yes and no answers only. No
sampled item was used to develop the prompt.

## Switchboard comparison {#sec-switchboard}

I compared the generated repairs with RSR in NXT Switchboard, restricted
to one word replaced by one word, where the measures below are defined.
After shared words at the start and end are removed, one word must be left
on each side; nested disfluencies, repetitions, fragments and filled pauses
are excluded. This leaves 1,858 of about 28,000 Switchboard disfluencies
and 3,249 of the 3,489 training items.^[The synthetic extraction sometimes
cuts a multi-word repair short, such as "ninety, one hundred" becoming
"ninety → one"; these cases remain in the figures.] Of 100 Switchboard
items drawn at random, I judged 94 to be RSR, 3 not and 3 unclear.

The measures follow
[SPACER](https://aclanthology.org/2025.cmcl-1.19/), with small differences
in implementation: word frequency (SUBTLEXus), semantic distance (GloVe),
phonemic distance (CMU pronunciations), and surprisal under GPT-2 small,
given the sentence up to the changed word.


# Results {#sec-results}

## Quality by category

@tbl-results sets each category against the thresholds.

| category | passed checks | correct in meaning | natural |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| content word | 93.2% | 14/14 | 14/14 |
| name | 95.5% | 11/11 | 14/14 |
| number | 94.6% | 13/13 | 10/11 |
| temporal | 96.9% | 15/15 | 14/14 |
| tense | 96.1% | 15/15 | 14/14 |
| forwarding | 96.3% | 4/4 | 11/12 |
| edge label | 97.1% | 32/33 | **14/29** |
| *threshold* | *≥ 95%* | *≥ 90%* | *≥ 80%* |

: Automatic checks and manual annotation by category. Check rates are over
answered items, from one run per category (5,984 items for the first six,
377 for edge label). Annotation counts are yes / (yes + no) on 15 items per
category (34 for edge label), with unsure answers left out. Edge label was
annotated on a run with the same prompt as its check rate. {#tbl-results}

All six categories other than edge label pass both annotation thresholds.
The samples are small, though. With 15 items even a perfect score is
compatible with a true rate as low as 80% (95% Wilson interval), so the
annotation shows that no category is clearly failing but cannot rank them.

Content word and number fall just short of the check threshold. For content
word this is due to synonyms, which only this category can produce; without
them it passes 96.5%. Since failing items are dropped, the shortfall costs
items but does not lower the quality of those kept. The model declined fewer
than ten of nearly 6,000 sentences. What the failures consist of is more
telling.  

::: {.callout}
Ill-formed SBN is rare (30 items). More often the model changed
something the repair did not ask for, for instance by putting the two
versions the wrong way round ("covered in pigeon, crow poop" for a gold
sentence about pigeon poop). The model finds it harder to change exactly
what the repair requires than to write well-formed SBN.
:::


## Edge label: the exception {#sec-edge}

Edge label was the hardest category to generate. It is the only one that
does not meet the thresholds through generation and automatic checks alone.
Its repairs pass the checks (97.1%) and are almost always correct in
meaning, but many do not sound natural. In the final round of iteration, of the 988 edge-label items that
passed the checks, I judged only 489 natural, about half.

No simple rule separates the natural items from the unnatural ones. Verbs
that express a direction rarely allow a natural swap (e.g., "A lion escaped to, from the zoo"). For other
verbs the judgement depends on tense and aspect. "Tom has gone from, to
Boston" also sounds odd because "has gone" is close to a fixed expression for
having left. No list of verbs could capture this.

Several rounds of prompt revision did not raise this share. The only way to
a usable set was therefore to read every item that passed the checks and
keep the natural ones. I expect that I need to do the same for dev/test sets.

## Comparison with Switchboard {#sec-switchboard-results}

The two sets are close in how far the replacement goes, but differ in what
is replaced and in which direction (@tbl-switchboard). Switchboard
replacements are mostly verbs, pronouns, conjunctions and determiners, and
a third of them change part of speech; the synthetic ones are mostly
numbers, names, verbs and prepositions, and almost all keep it. In
Switchboard the repair also tends to be less frequent and less predictable
than the word it replaces. The synthetic data show the opposite, which fits
how they were made: the repair is the word the PMB sentence was written
with, and the reparandum is invented afterwards. The gap is largest for
edge label and remains without it (median −0.41 bits).

| measure (median) | Switchboard | synthetic | Cliff's δ |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Δ frequency (Zipf) | −0.32 | +0.23 | +0.38 |
| semantic distance | 0.42 | 0.43 | −0.06 |
| phonemic distance | 3 | 3 | +0.15 |
| Δ surprisal (bits) | +0.44 | −0.69 | −0.30 |

: One-word replacements. Δ is repair minus reparandum. Words missing from a
resource are left out of that measure; for Δ frequency these are a sixth
of the synthetic items, mostly numbers, years and rare names. {#tbl-switchboard}

The data therefore suit training and testing a parser for the proposed
representation, but they are not a sample of conversational RSR. Before
the findings are extended to natural speech, the parser should be checked
on observed RSR.

# Limitations and next steps {#sec-limits}

The evidence behind this answer has at least three main limits.

- **One annotator.** All annotation and the edge-label selection rest on my
  intuition. Considering that 1. I am not a native speaker of English, 2. intra-annotator drift exists, and 3. I only annotated the dataset once, the quality of the dataset can be questionable.
- **Samples and upper bounds.** Apart from edge label, no category was read
  in full. There might exist data that in fact be wrong but can pass the structural check. 
- **Written source.** PMB sentences are short written text, and the repairs
  are constructed, not observed. Natural here means acceptable to a fluent
  speaker, which the Switchboard comparison can complement but not replace.


Three steps come next. I will first add editing expressions ("I mean", "no",
"no wait", "actually") by script to a fixed share of the items (10%), which gives
matched pairs of the same repair with and without an expression. "Sorry" is
kept back for the test set as an unseen expression. 

After that, I plan to mix the synthesised RSR data with PMB Train Gold and upload it to HuggingFace as the train set. 

I will then build the dev and test sets from PMB's own
splits with the same prompts and checks.

## Questions for my supervisors {#sec-questions}

1. Should dev and test be annotated more heavily than train, for example in
   full? They are smaller, and an error there affects the evaluation
   directly.
